title: US wait times for cancer surgeries are getting longer and longer
gist: A JAMA Surgery study of 2.7 million US cancer patients (2012-2023) found surgery wait times rose for all six major cancer types studied, with breast cancer going from 34 to 45 days and colon from 20 to 31 days, and the authors link the deterioration to healthcare consolidation funneling patients into high-volume academic centers that have become bottlenecks.

insights.claim: A JAMA Surgery study covering over 2.7 million US patients diagnosed with non-metastatic stage I-III cancers between 2012 and 2023 found wait times to surgery increased for all six cancer types examined and incrementally across every sub-period.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: A decade-long, monotonic degradation across every cancer type is a structural capacity signal, not noise — relevant to hospital operators, ASC operators and health-system capex theses.

insights.claim: US breast cancer surgery wait times rose from 34 days in 2012-2015 to 45 days in 2022-2023, and colon cancer from 20 days to 31 days — roughly a 32 percent and 55 percent increase respectively.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: The highest-volume cancer surgeries show the largest relative delay growth, pointing to demand overload in the most routine, highest-throughput procedures.
insights.quote: For breast cancer, wait times went from 34 days in 2012–2015 to 45 days in 2022–2023. For colon cancer, they went from 20 days to 31 days.

insights.claim: Lung cancer surgery waits rose from 41 to 53 days, pancreatic from 23 to 32 days, gastric from 35 to 49 days and esophageal from 38 to 48 days across the 2012-2015 to 2022-2023 comparison.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Delays worsened even in aggressive cancers where timing is most clinically consequential — a quality metric that payers and accreditation bodies may start pricing.

insights.claim: The share of patients experiencing prolonged waits of 30 or more days and 'extreme' waits of 60 or more days increased across every cancer type studied, meaning the tail of the distribution worsened alongside the median.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Tail risk matters more than averages for outcomes and malpractice exposure; systems reporting only mean wait times understate the problem.

insights.claim: The wait-time increases occurred as US healthcare systems consolidated and expanded, funneling more patients toward centralized high-volume treatment centers, particularly academic institutions — creating patient bottlenecks that may negate the quality benefit of specialized care.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Central thesis against the consolidation-improves-outcomes narrative used to justify hospital M&A; regulators and antitrust reviewers now have a throughput-based counterargument.
insights.quote: These increases in wait times occurred as healthcare systems in the US have consolidated and expanded, funneling more patients to centralized, high-volume treatment centers, particularly academic institutions.

insights.claim: The study authors argue that routing uncomplicated cases such as breast-conserving surgery or straightforward colectomy to high-volume centers introduces avoidable delay without matching clinical benefit, and that referral triage should reserve big centers for complex or uncommon cases.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Implies a structural case for community hospitals and ambulatory surgery centers retaining routine oncology volume — a reversal of the referral-upstream trend.

insights.claim: Centralized cancer centers could compress wait times by increasing patient capacity and optimizing scheduling and referral systems rather than by turning volume away, per the study authors' recommendations.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Direct demand signal for surgical scheduling, capacity-optimization and referral-management software vendors selling into academic health systems.

insights.claim: Longer cancer surgery waits fall disproportionately on uninsured or Medicaid patients, Black patients relative to white, lower-income patients, and those traveling longer distances to a treatment center.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Equity-linked quality metrics are increasingly tied to reimbursement; systems with skewed wait-time distributions face growing payer and regulatory scrutiny.

insights.claim: Timeliness is treated as a core healthcare quality metric and delays in cancer surgery have been linked to reduced survival rates plus increased patient anxiety and distress, so worsening waits directly erode measured care quality even as treatments improve.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Therapeutic advances and system throughput are moving in opposite directions — a headwind that could blunt the realized benefit of new oncology drugs and devices.
